# U5-C04 - Ludwig Boltzmann and James Clerk Maxwell

Unit 5 | All competition levels | public-student | Rule 5.c.v, printed B57

## Learning objectives
Connect microscopic motion to macroscopic gas properties; read a speed distribution; use a small counting model to explain multiplicity; distinguish statistical entropy from a vague claim of disorder.

## Prerequisites and how to read this chapter
Units 1–4 introduced temperature, heat, work, phase changes, particles and energy conservation. This chapter explains how those ideas developed. Historical terminology can differ from modern terminology. All numerical data below are original teaching models, not reconstructed historical measurements. No quotation is attributed to a scientist unless explicitly identified as a quotation; this unit uses original paraphrases.

## A gas looks smooth because it contains many particles
A pressure gauge gives a fairly steady reading even though gas molecules strike a wall at many separate times. A thermometer gives one temperature even though particles do not all have the same speed. Kinetic theory links these macroscopic measurements to microscopic motion. A macroscopic property describes the sample at the scale of a laboratory measurement; a microscopic description refers to individual particles and their states.

The challenge is enormous: even a small gas sample contains too many particles to follow individually. Statistical reasoning asks about distributions and likely collective behavior instead. It does not mean abandoning physical laws or guessing without evidence. It means using a description appropriate to a large population, much as a class’s score distribution contains more information than its average alone.

## Maxwell: replace a single speed with a distribution
James Clerk Maxwell lived from 1831 to 1879. Alongside his work on electromagnetism, he developed a statistical treatment of gases. His 1860 papers on the dynamical theory of gases introduced the molecular velocity distribution associated with his name. Later work by Maxwell and Boltzmann developed the subject further. The combined name Maxwell–Boltzmann does not prove they wrote one joint paper or performed one shared experiment. [H10,H11]

In an equilibrium gas, some particles move slowly, many have intermediate speeds, and some move very fast. Collisions change individual speeds and directions; a particle is not assigned permanently to a “fast group.” At steady temperature the distribution can remain stable even while its individual members change. This is a powerful distinction between an unchanging statistical pattern and frozen microscopic motion.

Read a speed graph carefully. The horizontal axis shows speed, not temperature. The vertical axis indicates the number or fraction in a speed interval, or a density that must be interpreted with the interval width. For equal-width histogram bins, taller bars mean more particles in that interval. The most populated bin is not automatically the average speed, and the largest individual speed is not the position of the peak.

For the same ideal-gas species, raising temperature shifts the distribution toward higher speeds and broadens it. Some slow particles remain; not every hot-gas particle is faster than every cooler-gas particle. The curves overlap. Comparing different gases adds the effect of molecular mass: equal temperature means equal average translational kinetic energy in the ideal-gas model, not equal speed distributions for all species. No speed formula or calculus is needed for these comparisons.

## Boltzmann: probability and the second law
Ludwig Boltzmann lived from 1844 to 1906 and worked extensively on kinetic theory and the statistical foundations of thermodynamics. His 1877 paper connected entropy to the number of microscopic possibilities compatible with a macroscopic description. [H12,H13] This added a microscopic explanation to the entropy framework associated with Clausius; it did not erase the macroscopic theory or claim that energy conservation had become optional.

A macrostate specifies coarse properties, such as how many particles occupy each half of a box. A microstate gives the detailed assignment of individual labeled particles in our simplified model. Real microscopic states also involve positions and momenta, but a left/right model is enough to illustrate multiplicity, the number of compatible detailed arrangements. The labels are bookkeeping devices in this teaching model, not a derivation of quantum statistics.

Take four independent labeled tokens A, B, C and D. Each is equally likely to be in either half of a box. There are 2×2×2×2=16 possible assignments. Only one puts all four on the left. Six put two on each side: AB, AC, AD, BC, BD or CD on the left, with the others on the right. The balanced macrostate is more likely than the specified all-left macrostate because more detailed assignments produce it, not because each particle “wants balance.”

## What a tiny model can and cannot prove
The model demonstrates why counting possibilities matters. It does not say that four tokens will always split evenly. Indeed, ten of the sixteen assignments are not exactly two-and-two. When enormous numbers of particles are considered, relative deviations from the most probable bulk behavior become much smaller. That is why ordinary gas expansion and mixing have a reliable natural direction on everyday scales even though microscopic descriptions are statistical.

Entropy is related to the multiplicity of accessible microscopic states subject to physical constraints. “Disorder” can be an informal memory aid, but visual messiness is not a measurement of entropy. A shuffled-looking picture might conceal strong constraints, while a smooth-looking gas can have an enormous number of microscopic arrangements. Energy, volume, particle number and the specified model matter. This unit uses counting and qualitative comparisons rather than a logarithmic entropy formula.

Boltzmann’s constant k_B links a per-particle energy scale to thermodynamic temperature. Its SI value is exactly 1.380649×10⁻²³ J/K; k_B T therefore has energy units. It is not itself a temperature, and k_B T is not a universal formula for the entire internal energy of any object. [H04] The modern notation and metrological definition are later refinements, so the constant’s name should not be read as a claim that Boltzmann personally established every modern detail.

## Maxwell’s demon: inspect a hidden boundary
Maxwell described a selective molecular gatekeeper in an 1867 letter; the thought experiment appeared publicly in his 1871 book Theory of Heat. [H14] Imagine a tiny agent that allows faster particles toward one side and slower particles toward the other. Starting from a uniform gas, such sorting seems to create a hot side and a cold side without the usual work requirement. That apparent loophole probes what the second law assumes about microscopic control.

The demon is a thought experiment, not a real creature discovered in a gas. A complete modern account must include the physical controller, its information handling and its restoration for repeated operation. Looking only at the sorted gas hides part of the entropy accounting. It is too simple to claim that merely looking always supplies a fixed amount of heat; measurement, storage, feedback and resetting must be treated as a complete physical process. This unit asks only for the boundary insight, not advanced information-thermodynamics equations.

## Connections to previous units and applications
In Unit 1, temperature was a collective property rather than the speed of one molecule. In Unit 2, gas pressure arose from particle interactions with boundaries. Unit 3’s conduction can be interpreted through microscopic energy exchange. Unit 4’s entropy constraints now gain a statistical perspective. These are teaching connections among concepts, not a claim that the four units were discovered in that order.

Diffusion of an odor through air and the persistence of a stable thermometer reading despite collisions illustrate why distributions are useful. A simulation can follow many particles or tokens, but its rules must be stated. An artificial rule that pushes every token toward balance would bake the conclusion into the model rather than demonstrate how counting produces a probability difference.

## Important terminology
Kinetic theory: particle-motion account of bulk behavior. Distribution: how a population is spread over values. Macrostate: coarse description. Microstate: detailed state consistent with a model. Multiplicity: number of compatible microstates. Boltzmann constant: energy-per-temperature conversion constant, J/K. Thought experiment: reasoning through a hypothetical arrangement.

## Worked example: Count an illustrative macrostate

**Given:** Four independent labeled tokens each have two equally likely sides. Six assignments have two on each side.

**Find:** Probability of a two-and-two split.

**Formula:** Probability=favorable assignments/total assignments.

**Substitution:** p=6/2⁴.

**Calculation:** 2⁴=16; 6/16=0.375.

**Final answer:** p=37.5%.

**Physical interpretation:** The balanced macrostate is the single most numerous category, but is not guaranteed in a four-token trial.

## Worked example: Read a speed-bin table

**Given:** A toy sample of 100 particles has 8,32,40,16,4 particles in five ascending equal-width speed bins.

**Find:** Fraction in the two fastest bins.

**Formula:** Fraction=(count in selected bins)/(total count).

**Substitution:** (16+4)/100.

**Calculation:** 20/100=0.20.

**Final answer:** 20% are in the two fastest bins.

**Physical interpretation:** The distribution gives information hidden by a single temperature reading. These are illustrative counts, not Maxwell’s measured data.

## Common historical and scientific confusions
Equal temperature does not mean equal speed for every particle. Maxwell and Boltzmann did not jointly discover every named result. Boltzmann did not first introduce the term entropy. More probable does not mean certain for a tiny sample. Maxwell’s demon does not demonstrate a free, endlessly repeatable violation of the second law.

## Application and safe investigation
Use four labeled paper tokens and fair coin flips to assign left/right positions, repeating trials without selectively discarding outcomes. Compare observed frequencies with the 16 equally likely assignments; differences in a short trial are expected. Keep tokens on a desk rather than treating loose beads or gases as a required physical experiment. A data-only alternative uses the supplied assignment table.

## Chapter summary
Maxwell’s gas theory used distributions rather than one molecular speed. Boltzmann connected thermodynamic behavior and entropy to microscopic possibilities. Simple counting builds intuition, while careful system boundaries prevent the demon thought experiment from becoming a false perpetual-motion claim.

## Chapter review
1. How can a stable distribution coexist with changing molecular speeds?
2. Why does multiplicity refer to a macrostate rather than the visual neatness of a picture?
3. What must a complete account of Maxwell’s demon include?
